shows.title: this is a show about grief
shows.dates_note: Venue's page says the show is "Opening Friday, Sept. 11th, 2026 / Exhibit will run through early October" with no exact closing date given.
shows.description:
Ghost Gallery's latest open-call group show takes grief as its subject in the broadest possible sense — not just death, but climate anxiety, lost rights, missed connections, and the slow-burn unease of the present moment. It's part of a run of themed group exhibitions the gallery has staged through its 20th-anniversary year, built entirely from an open call rather than a curated artist list.

Given the open submission format, expect a genuinely wide range of media: paintings, drawings, prints, ceramics, sculpture, zines, and small-scale wearable and text-based work, since the gallery's call specifically invited work across all of those categories with no thematic filter beyond the prompt itself. That structure tends to produce shows that are uneven but personal — more diaristic than polished, which suits the subject matter.

A portion of proceeds from the show goes to grief-care and climate-justice nonprofits, continuing Ghost Gallery's habit of tying its exhibitions to a charitable component. Given the gallery's small footprint inside Pacific Place, this is best approached as a browsing show rather than a single big statement — worth a stop on a Belltown or downtown gallery circuit rather than a dedicated destination trip.

shows.title: Warp, Weft and Landlines
shows.description:
Allison Collins paints landscapes that refuse to sit still: her abstracted fields, shorelines, and horizons are built up with the textural logic of quilting, patchwork planes of saturated red, gold, green, and blue standing in for remembered places rather than depicting any single one. The paintings move between a far horizon line and a flattened, all-over surface, holding both spatial depth and pattern-like flatness at once.

A UW and Otis College-trained painter and Whitney Museum fellowship recipient whose work has represented the U.S. Embassy in Bucharest, Collins has spent years refining this quilt-and-landscape vocabulary; Warp, Weft and Landlines is the next chapter in that ongoing series, emphasizing the textile metaphor in the title itself. It's a good show for anyone who likes their landscape painting a little unmoored from geography — more about the feeling of travel and memory than any actual place.
shows.reception: Opens First Thursday, October 1, 6-8pm with the artist in attendance

shows.title: Timeless Euphoria
shows.description:
Timeless Euphoria is Columbia City Gallery's fall community exhibit, one of the open-call shows the co-op runs alongside its juried and member exhibitions to give a broader circle of local artists wall space. As a community exhibit rather than a themed juried show, it tends to gather a loose mix of media and subject matter from artists connected to the gallery and the Columbia City area rather than presenting a single curatorial thesis.

Community exhibits like this one are where Columbia City Gallery's identity as a cooperative really shows: the work is unvetted by an outside juror, so the range of skill level and approach is wider than in the juried show, and the pleasure of it is often in the surprises and the neighborhood feel rather than a tightly argued theme. It runs concurrently with Shifting Horizons, the gallery's autumn member exhibit, with a joint artists' reception on October 10.
shows.reception: Saturday, October 10, 5-7pm (joint reception with Shifting Horizons)

shows.title: Shifting Horizons
shows.description:
Shifting Horizons is Columbia City Gallery's fall member exhibit, the recurring show reserved for the gallery's own roster of cooperative member-artists rather than an open call or juried pool. Where the concurrent Timeless Euphoria draws from the wider community, this one is a chance to see what the gallery's regulars — the working artists who run the space themselves — have been making lately.

Member shows at artist-run cooperatives like this one tend to read as a loose group portrait of the gallery's own program: painting, printmaking, mixed media, glass, and craft-based work sitting side by side without a single unifying theme beyond membership itself. It shares an opening reception with Timeless Euphoria on October 10, making that Saturday evening the moment to see both fall shows together in the gallery's Columbia City storefront.
shows.reception: Saturday, October 10, 5-7pm (joint reception with Timeless Euphoria)

shows.title: The Threshold of Thought and Appearance
shows.description:
Seattle-based Ko Kirk Yamahira has spent years turning painting inside out — literally. His process involves pulling individual warp threads back out of stretched canvas, one at a time, until what was once a flat painted surface becomes a hanging, draping sculptural form. This show, his latest solo outing with studio e, centers on a large C-shaped structure built from this subtractive unthreading, with a cluster of smaller works surrounding it.

The pieces on view — hand-dyed canvas partially unwoven into loose, gauzy structures in warm sunset tones — read less as objects than as records of a slow, meditative undoing. Yamahira doesn't fix a single orientation for his work; pieces get reconfigured each time they're installed, so the same body of work can look different from one showing to the next. The centerpiece invites viewers to step inside the unwound form itself, surrounded by floating threads, which turns the show's central idea — surface becoming form, painting becoming structure — into something felt physically rather than just observed.

Yamahira's work has been collected by the Frye Art Museum, Bellevue Arts Museum, and major tech companies' corporate collections, and this exhibition extends a practice he's been refining since his first solo museum show at the Frye in 2018. It's a good entry point for anyone curious about where process-based abstraction can go once a painting stops being asked to stay a painting.

shows.title: Intwined
shows.description:
Rebecca Woodhouse builds her collages from cut-apart linoprints and salvaged vintage neckties, sourced from a WWII survivor's decades-spanning private collection, weaving traditionally masculine and feminine materials into a single layered surface. The necktie work began as a pandemic-era pivot away from large-scale painting and grew into an ongoing exploration of memory, inheritance, and generational bonds.

Shown alongside richly textured paintings that combine dozens of layers of linocut work with painted line, the collages read as a quiet argument against Modernism's gendered material hierarchies — repurposing a garment coded as masculine into a medium for tenderness and remembrance. It's intimate, handmade work that rewards close looking at the seams and gaps where materials meet.
shows.reception: First Thursday Art Walk, October 1, 5-8pm; Reception & Artist Talk, Saturday October 24, 4-6pm

shows.title: In Between: A Cross and a Hardgrave
shows.dates_note: Venue's Future Exhibitions listing prints the dates as "October 10 – November 15, 2025," but the reception days given (Saturday Oct 10 / Sunday Oct 11) only align with the calendar in 2026, and the show is listed as upcoming on a page updated Sept 2026 — dates recorded here as Oct 10 – Nov 15, 2026.
shows.description:
In Between pairs two Pacific Northwest painters, Tim Cross and Robert Hardgrave, in solo presentations co-curated with Koplin Del Rio, the Seattle gallery that has partnered with AMcE on cross-programmed shows before (including 2025's LAnd SEA). Cross builds abstract compositions from paint, colored liquids, and transferred imagery, blending drawn organic forms with traced architectural and mechanical fragments — work that reads as a kind of visual ecosystem where nature and construction bleed into each other.

Hardgrave, a longtime fixture of AMcE's program, works in acrylic transfer, collage, and mixed media, building densely patterned figures and scenes out of layered imagery; his recent panels shown here move toward smaller, concrete-textured surfaces alongside his signature large transfer paintings. Shown together, the two artists' very different working methods — Cross's atmospheric abstraction and Hardgrave's collaged figuration — offer a useful contrast in how Northwest painters process image and material.

The show opens with a media preview and an artist reception the following day, a fitting kickoff for a two-person exhibition built on dialogue between studios.

shows.title: Dwelling In the Light
shows.dates_note: Homepage says only "Coming in October" for this show; no exact opening or closing date published yet.
shows.description:
Lisa Snow Lady's paintings and mixed-media collages work in a soft, saturated palette — acrylic scenes and paper collages built up on panel that favor gentle atmosphere over hard edges. Titles like "Still Water," "Spot Light," and "In Soft Light" point to a recurring interest in the quality of illumination itself: how light settles over water, forest, and quiet interior moments.

Several works combine painted passages with collaged paper on panel, giving the surfaces a layered, tactile quality distinct from straight acrylic on canvas. Local landmarks make an appearance too — a small panel titled "Strong Light (Ballard Locks)" suggests a Pacific Northwest sensibility grounded in specific place alongside the more atmospheric, dreamlike pieces.

This will be Lynn Hanson Gallery's next show after its current run, following the gallery's pattern of monthly rotating solo and two-person exhibitions in its Pioneer Square space.

venue.name: Lynn Hanson Gallery
hours: First Thursdays 5pm to 8pm and by appointment

shows.title: Filter: PCNW's Benefit Auction Preview Exhibition
shows.description:
Every fall, Photographic Center Northwest hangs a preview of the prints going up for bid at its benefit auction, and the result is one of the more eclectic group shows in the city's photo calendar. Rather than being organized around a theme, the exhibition is a survey of the medium's range: intimate portraiture sits near quiet landscape work, documentary reportage, concert photography, and hand-processed alternative work, with contributors spanning celebrated names and PCNW's own teaching community.

The checklist mixes generations and approaches deliberately — expect gelatin silver prints alongside contemporary color work, a Berenice Abbott or Richard Avedon-adjacent sensibility next to newer voices working in ecological and social documentary modes. It's less a curated argument than a snapshot of what PCNW's extended community is making and collecting right now, which is exactly the point: every print here was donated to support the organization's education and darkroom programs.

For visitors, the appeal is partly the gallery-going and partly the game of guessing which images will draw bids at the October 16 auction. It's a good entry point for anyone curious about PCNW's programming beyond its darkrooms and certificate courses, and a chance to see strong single prints by dozens of photographers in one room rather than a single artist's survey.

shows.title: Shifting Forms: Masks of Today
shows.dates_note: Site presents this as the current gallery feature (published Aug 8, 2026, homepage banner links directly to it) but publishes no opening or closing date for the run.
shows.description:
Shifting Forms gathers a wide range of contemporary Northwest Coast masks under one roof, moving from portrait masks to transformation pieces depicting animals, ancestors, and supernatural beings. The strength of the show is its range of hands: David A. Boxley's crisp Tsimshian carving sits alongside Shawn Aster's bold formline animal masks, Phil Gray's intricate "From the Sky," and Raymond Shaw's large-scale "Kolus Transformation," giving visitors a genuine cross-section of how differently artists across nations approach the same basic form.

What distinguishes the gallery's framing of the show is its insistence that these are not static objects — the accompanying text is explicit that these masks belong to living ceremonial traditions of dance, potlatch, and storytelling, and that displaying them for sale doesn't strip that context away. That's a useful lens for a commercial gallery show: rather than presenting the masks purely as sculpture, it asks viewers to think about movement, sound, and performance even while the pieces sit still on the wall.

For anyone new to Northwest Coast art, this is an unusually good survey to walk into cold — dozens of masks by more than a dozen artists, spanning price points and generations, gathered specifically because they share a form rather than a single hand or nation.

shows.title: Sky of the Mind
shows.artist: Karey Kessler, Soo Hong, Kalina Winska, and Teresa Getty
shows.description:
Taking its title from a phrase the Northwest School painter Morris Graves used to describe an inner, spiritual landscape, this four-artist show gathers painters who treat abstraction as a way of mapping interior states rather than depicting the visible world. Each artist arrives at that territory from a different angle: Karey Kessler borrows the visual language of maps and cartography to link the external world to the internal one, while Soo Hong works in fluid washes of watercolor, ink, and acrylic on Korean muslin to trace the blurry line between memory and belonging.

Kalina Winska's graphite and colored-pencil drawings on yupo draw from weather systems and climate data to build speculative, semi-technological landscapes, and Teresa Getty's layered oil paintings sit at the intersection of intention, memory, and intuition, resisting a single fixed reading. Despite their different materials — paper, muslin, yupo, canvas — all four practices share an interest in painting as a tool for thinking rather than recording.

It's a quietly ambitious pairing of local abstraction, useful for anyone curious about how Northwest painters are still working through the region's long tradition of landscape-as-metaphor.
shows.reception: Opening/First Thursday Art Walk, October 1, 5-8pm; Artist Talk Saturday, October 24, 2pm
